title: Pseudorandomness and reproducibility
lead: Separate engines, distributions, seeds and saved datasets; test promised properties without inventing guarantees.
why: A generator helps discover defects and build experiments, but random data does not replace boundary cases. Replaying a defect requires the algorithm, environment and actual data as well as a seed.
objectives: Validate the seed domain before conversion.
Test repeatability with identical state histories.
prerequisites: Modules 1–3: validated input, functions, vector, records, references and lifetimes.
Direct learning dependencies: cpp.associative-containers. New constructs are explained before the task.

sections.title: A deterministic sequence and state
paragraphs: A pseudorandom engine computes an output from its state and updates that state. Equal initial states and equal call histories produce equal streams. The output may look random without being physical randomness. An extra call, even for debugging output, shifts all later values.

A seed initializes state under the engine’s rules. Copying an engine copies state rather than magically creating an independent source. Recreating an engine from the same seed at every step restarts its sequence. Create one engine for a series and explicitly define where a new reproducible experiment begins.

sections.title: A named engine versus a library choice
paragraphs: std::mt19937 has standard-specified parameters, and C++20 specifies a check value for its default-constructed engine’s 10000th output. This enables an exact cross-environment check of that stream. default_random_engine is an implementation choice, so sharing its type name does not prove two platforms use the same algorithm.

Exactly 10000 calls in the worked example yield 4123659995. This is a narrow assertion about that engine, not every <random> generator. Do not transfer that precision to mapping into a desired range: a distribution is a separate step with its own contract and potentially its own state.

sections.title: A distribution specifies a law and range
paragraphs: uniform_int_distribution<int>(lo,hi) produces uniform integers over a closed range, including both endpoints. Check lo≤hi before constructing it. The lab bounds endpoints to −1000…1000 to avoid relying on int extremes. lo==hi is valid: every result is the range’s single value.

The algorithm mapping engine outputs to a distribution can differ between standard libraries. The same mt19937 and seed therefore need not yield the same distributed array on libc++ and libstdc++. This lesson checks range, length and replay within one implementation; cross-environment defect replay uses the saved actual-number file.

sections.title: Why a remainder can introduce bias
paragraphs: Imagine a uniform source over 0…7 and a desired output over 0…2. Remainder modulo three gives three preimages each for zero and one, but only two for two. The output is therefore biased despite the uniform source. A small sample can accidentally hide this structural bias.

Discarding six and seven before taking the remainder leaves two preimages per result in this toy model. That explains rejection sampling without directing you to implement a production distribution. A standard distribution expresses the intent more clearly, but still needs valid bounds and a reproducibility policy.

sections.title: Replay is a controlled experiment
paragraphs: The lab creates two engines with one seed and two distributions with matching parameters, then makes the same calls in the same order. The arrays must match within the current implementation. Save samples.txt, repeat.txt, compiler/runtime and parameters. Do not infer replay solely from a printed “yes”; compare the actual files.

Different seeds need not produce different observed arrays: n=0 makes both empty, lo==hi makes every value identical, and short samples can coincide too. A mandatory “different seeds, different arrays” test would invent a guarantee. List the promised properties before testing plausible-sounding assumptions.

sections.title: Properties, frequencies and false conclusions
paragraphs: Check exact length, each value’s bounds and replay of the corresponding runs. all_of is true on an empty range, so verify length separately. These checks do not prove uniformity: always printing lo can satisfy them. Explaining the actual distribution choice and inspecting source are part of the manual rubric.

A histogram helps explore data, but a uniform law does not require perfectly equal counts in every finite sample. A statistical test needs a hypothesis, sample size and false-positive policy. This lesson does not substitute an arbitrary threshold; it checks deterministic contract properties and preserves observations.

sections.title: Test generation and security boundaries
paragraphs: Random cases supplement empty, minimum, maximum, all-equal and already ordered inputs rather than replacing them. Save the seed of a discovered failure, then shrink the actual data to a comprehensible counterexample. A small fixed regression case is usually more useful than hoping to rediscover the defect randomly.

mt19937 is not intended for cryptographic tasks. This browser runtime does not treat random_device as a guaranteed system-entropy source. Do not use the educational generator for security-critical values. Sampling without replacement and shuffling have their own contracts; sorting with a “random comparator” is not a safe substitute because it violates ordering requirements.

sections.title: Lab artifacts and the next experiment
paragraphs: Before running, record n, seed, endpoints and expected logical results. Afterward check both file shapes, line counts, bounds and equality. Keep source and environment details. Across native and WASI, compare the promised properties; different raw distributed numbers alone are not a runtime defect.

The next lesson uses fixed data to compare algorithms and separate clocks to observe cost. Saved inputs let you separate computation differences from generation differences. Input class, program version, verification method and raw samples become part of a reproducible engineering experiment.

workedExamples.title: A standardized engine and an explicit check
workedExamples.purpose: Distinguish an engine’s specified sequence from a distribution’s transformation.
steps: mt19937 names a particular algorithm with fixed parameters; default_random_engine is not that contract.
e stores changing state. Each e() advances the sequence.
The loop makes exactly 10000 calls; value holds the last result, not a sum.
The mt19937 behavior check in the C++20 draft specifies 4123659995, which fits result_type.
This neither assesses cryptographic strength nor specifies a uniform_int_distribution sequence.

steps: Two engines use seed 2026; both distributions have range −3…3.

x==y checks replay within the current library; bounded checks every element independently.
Check length 512 separately: an empty sequence could otherwise satisfy all_of.

laboratory.title: Laboratory: Pseudorandomness and reproducibility
laboratory.catalogGoal: Separate engines, distributions, seeds and saved datasets; test promised properties without inventing guarantees.
laboratory.challenge: Read n seed lo hi with no extra tokens: n=0…128, seed=0…4294967295, −1000<=lo<=hi<=1000. Create two identically initialized mt19937 engines and two uniform_int_distribution objects; save n integers on separate lines in samples.txt and repeat.txt. Print count N, repeatable yes, bounded yes on separate lines. Both files must exist, agree and satisfy the bounds; exact cross-library sequences are unspecified. Invalid input gives invalid.
